Noise-free 64 x 64 synthetic test: the positive test object has a lowest plotted contour at about 1% of its highest contour. Its dirty beam comes from an untapered circular aperture whose diameter is about two-thirds of the full rectangular aperture extent, with a 40-degree sector removed to simulate an unsampled observing interval and the central DC term retained. The largest positive non-central beam sample is 56% of the peak and the largest negative sidelobe is 38%. Modified CLEAN uses \(T_c=0.55\) and 17 iterations. A comparison CLEAN with a 15% central beam spike uses 2,000 subtractions. Both density files are visually free of stripes and are described as comparable, while the modified result has lower RMS error against the original object; the paper gives no RMS values. Standard CLEAN leaves visibly separated components in the extended regions. The figures compare unconvolved density files so that clean-beam smoothing does not hide differences between deconvolution algorithms.

Noisy 256 x 256 synthetic test: the object combines point sources with extended emission; the paper displays only its central 64 x 64 region. The dirty map uses a circular sinc-function beam with noise whose standard deviation is 1% of the peak, and the lowest displayed contour is 3% of the peak. The modified density file visually reproduces both the compact and extended structure, whereas standard CLEAN reproduces the narrow sources but the authors judge the extended area to be very poorly reproduced. No iteration count or scalar error is given for this test.

Analytical work estimates: for an image with \(M\) pixels, the paper approximates standard CLEAN work as \(N_s \approx 2Q_sM\), where \(Q_s\) is its iteration count. Modified CLEAN is estimated as \(N_m \approx Q_mM(4\log(M)/2+4)\), comprising four FFTs plus density-file addition, complex multiplication, trimming, and subtraction per iteration. A corresponding Clark CLEAN expression includes major-cycle count, minor-cycle count, and beam-patch area. The authors derive iteration-count expressions showing that modified CLEAN becomes relatively more favorable as the source covers more beam areas or a larger fraction of the image. These are algorithmic operation models, not timings, and the logarithm base and FFT constants depend on implementation details.

papers.title: The Noncoplanar Baselines Effect in Radio Interferometry: The W-Projection Algorithm

dynamic_range: Dynamic-range definitions: DR1 is peak brightness divided by the median absolute deviation from the image median. DR2 is peak brightness divided by the absolute value of the strongest nearby negative feature around a bright source. DR1 is a robust global image measure, while DR2 is sensitive to coherent source-local artifacts. The paper does not report RMSE, PSNR, SSIM, or a source-catalog photometric error.

Dynamic range and runtime: Standard two-dimensional Fourier transformation achieved DR1 = 1,570 and DR2 = 2.8, with 27 s per residual calculation and 216 s total deconvolution time. A 9 by 9 uvw-facet run reached DR1 = 12,580 and DR2 = 40, with 1,348 s per residual calculation and 30,488 s total. W-projection with 64 w-planes reached higher DR1 = 18,198 and DR2 = 524, with 83 s of kernel initialization, 607 s per residual calculation, and 3,161 s total. Thus this representative higher-dynamic-range w-projection run took about one tenth the total time of the 9 by 9 facet run. With 256 planes, w-projection reached the table's best DR1 = 50,888 and DR2 = 984, with 231 s initialization, 507 s per residual calculation, and 5,419 s total.

Scaling and tradeoffs: Across 8-256 w-planes, w-projection kernel-initialization time rises from 9 to 231 s and dynamic range improves, while residual-calculation time remains roughly flat at 671-507 s. The authors summarize w-projection as about 20 times slower than an uncorrected two-dimensional transform for this field because its typical 30 by 30 complex convolution region performs about 24 times the inner-loop work of 9 by 9 real gridding. At comparable dynamic range it is about an order of magnitude faster than uvw-space faceting. They report about a factor of 30 advantage in residual-calculation time and about a factor of 3 in error performance over facets, both in favor of w-projection; the overall advantage is smaller because faceting can skip empty facets early in CLEAN and has favorable minor-cycle scaling.

snr: Noise sweep: Gaussian visibility noise was added to an M51 model scaled to \(0.30\lambda/D\). The theoretical image-plane SNR is defined as the peak of the clean-beam-convolved model divided by image-plane noise. Maximum entropy began significantly overestimating flux at SNR as high as 100, whereas CLEAN, Maximum Emptiness, and Multiscale CLEAN retained accurate flux estimates down to SNR about 4; Högbom CLEAN remained reasonably accurate in integrated flux even below SNR 1. At low SNR, reconstructed dynamic range flattened near 4 as thermal noise dominated, while high-SNR curves began flattening because of deconvolution error. For a 2:1 band and four Taylor terms, Figure 4 reports dynamic range of about 100,000, reference-frequency peak-flux error of about 1 part in 1,000, absolute spectral-index error of about 0.01, and absolute curvature error of about 0.1. Errors decreased with increasing polynomial order until noise or a narrow bandwidth made extra terms an overfit. Because no noise was added, these are numerical best-case limits rather than observational sensitivity measurements.

3C286 dynamic-range test: Four EVLA snapshots over 90 minutes covered 1.02-2.1 GHz, with 800 MHz usable after radio-frequency-interference excision. The source was 14.4 Jy/beam at 1.5 GHz with spectral index -0.47, and all runs used one point-source scale. Raising the number of Taylor terms from one to four reduced RMS near 3C286 through 9 mJy, 1 mJy, 200 microJy, and 140 microJy; RMS measured 1 degree away was 1 mJy, 200 microJy, 85 microJy, and 80 microJy, against a 70 microJy thermal-noise estimate. Primary-beam and reported limits: Across a 2:1 EVLA band, the simulated primary beam adds an apparent spectral index of about -1.4 at its half-power point and can impose a dynamic-range limit near 1,000 if ignored. papers.title: Sparsity Averaging Reweighted Analysis (SARA): a novel algorithm for radio-interferometric imaging

snr: Controlled simulation context: Ground-truth M31 H II-region and 30 Doradus images are each 256 x 256 pixels with normalized brightness in [0.01, 1]. Visibilities follow the discrete measurement model with the primary beam set to identity. Random variable-density masks sample the half Fourier plane more densely at low spatial frequencies, omit the zero-frequency component, and range from 10% to 90% coverage. Complex Gaussian noise is added at 30 dB input SNR. The profiles are generic rather than tied to a telescope or observing frequency, and each plotted mean and one-standard-deviation error bar is computed over 100 simulations.

Reconstruction SNR definition: The quantitative fidelity metric is \(20 \log_{10}(\sigma_x/\sigma_{x-\hat{x}})\) dB, where \(\sigma_x\) is the standard deviation of the ground-truth image and \(\sigma_{x-\hat{x}}\) is the standard deviation of the reconstruction error. Input SNR uses the same form with the per-visibility noise standard deviation in the denominator. This is a ground-truth image-domain error score, not peak-to-RMS image dynamic range.

Coverage sweep: Against the directly run BP, BPDb8, TV, and IUWT benchmarks, SARA has the highest mean reconstruction SNR at every tested coverage for both images. For M31, the paper reports a gain over every other method of more than 6 dB at 10% coverage and at least 3 dB at the remaining coverages. For 30 Doradus, it reports at least a 2 dB gain at every coverage.

Representative 30%-coverage reconstructions: The individual M31 example reports 32.82 dB for BP, 33.70 dB for BPDb8, 32.12 dB for IUWT, 33.89 dB for TV, and 38.43 dB for SARA. The individual 30 Doradus example reports 16.67, 24.53, 17.87, 26.47, and 29.08 dB, respectively. These are example-image values at 30 dB input SNR, not the 100-run mean values digitized from the coverage plots.

Spread-spectrum illustration: A separate Cygnus A simulation uses 30% coverage, 30 dB input SNR, and a random-phase modulation in the measurement operator as a simplified spread-spectrum acquisition. Reported reconstruction SNRs are 16.6 dB for BP, 36.0 dB for BPDb8, 29.9 dB for BPIU, 28.7 dB for TV, and 40.2 dB for SARA. The paper presents this as an illustration, uses random phase rather than a physical quadratic w-term phase, and does not average the result over repeated trials.

Qualitative residual and artifact assessment: Residual images are the difference between the observed dirty image and the dirty image predicted from the reconstruction. SARA is judged to leave fewer background artifacts and smaller structural errors for M31, and to recover both point-like and extended 30 Doradus structure without the spurious points of BP/IUWT or the cartoon-like bias of TV. The paper notes that IUWT can produce a nearly flat residual despite larger ground-truth image error, and that all methods can give noise-like 30 Doradus residuals while differing materially in reconstruction SNR. These are visual assessments, not additional numerical metrics.
runtime: Runtime: MATLAB wall-clock times are measured on a 2.4 GHz Xeon quad-core processor and plotted in log10 seconds over the coverage sweep, again as means and one-standard-deviation error bars over 100 simulations. The paper describes SARA runtime as of the order of minutes and similar to TV in these tests and to published MS-CLEAN times. It does not tabulate exact times, specify the Xeon model, memory, MATLAB version, thread use, or visibility counts, and its MS-CLEAN comparison is cross-paper rather than a controlled same-hardware run.

Scope and missing benchmarks: The study uses synthetic, on-grid discrete Fourier samples and no measured interferometer data. Except for the simplified spread-spectrum illustration, it assumes a small field, identity primary beam, monochromatic non-polarized imaging, and no direction-dependent effects. It does not report flux-recovery error, source completeness, residual RMS in physical units, SSIM, memory use, or a direct CLEAN/MS-CLEAN runtime or fidelity benchmark. The authors identify continuous visibility handling, lower-level implementation, and parallel or distributed solvers as future work.

snr: Reconstruction SNR: the primary fidelity metric is \(20\log_{10}(\|x\|_2/\|x-\hat{x}\|_2)\), in dB, measured against the known noiseless model image. papers.title: HVOX: Scalable Interferometric Synthesis and Analysis of Spherical Sky Maps

nmse_nrmse: Accuracy metric and reference: The controlled accuracy experiment measures normalized mean square error (NMSE) between visibilities generated by direct evaluation of a point-source sky model and those generated by HVOX, chunked HVOX with a 500 MB per-partition limit, the stable DUCC W-gridder implementation labeled NIFTY, and NIFTY 2D with the w-term omitted. Requested error targets are swept for both direction-cosine and HEALPix source meshes.

Direction-cosine-grid accuracy: Monolithic HVOX follows the requested NMSE down to about 1e-9 in double precision. The paper attributes this floor to FINUFFT's default type-3 upsampling factor of 1.25, which lowers RAM and FFT size but limits accuracy to about nine digits. Chunked HVOX tracks the same curve but slightly misses the requested target because numerical errors accumulate when chunk outputs are summed; the authors propose compensating by tightening each sub-transform's target according to the number of blocks. NIFTY generally exceeds its requested accuracy by about one order of magnitude, while omitting the w-term in NIFTY 2D produces a much larger error that is insensitive to the requested target.

HEALPix accuracy and interpolation baseline: HVOX achieves essentially the same controllable NMSE on HEALPix as on a direction-cosine mesh. NIFTY requires bilinear interpolation from HEALPix to a direction-cosine grid before analysis; that interpolation introduces approximately 1% error, largely independent of the gridder's requested accuracy and comparable in the experiment to omitting the w-term. This comparison isolates the mesh-conversion loss rather than claiming an end-to-end restored-image improvement.
runtime: Runtime hardware and common setup: Runtime tests use one workstation with an Intel Core i9-10900X 10-core CPU and 128 GB DDR4 RAM. The default SKA-Low simulation has 251 antennas within a 1 km radius, 94,878 visibilities, one 50 kHz channel centered at 150 MHz, a 30-degree field of view, and a 360 x 360 direction-cosine image with 5.22 arcsec pixels. It samples three evenly spaced time intervals from an 8 h window to emphasize FFT cost, rather than processing every visibility from a full 8 h observation. HVOX uses 20 threads in the monolithic case and 5 per chunk in the chunked case, with a 500 MB maximum partition size.

Dense-grid runtime findings: For dense direction-cosine images, W-gridder is faster than HVOX v1, especially over roughly 1-10 km telescope radii. Monolithic HVOX exhausts memory at the largest configurations, whereas HVOX-500MB continues to the 100 km, 182.25-megapixel case and approaches W-gridder's analysis time there. Synthesis is slower than analysis for the NUFFT methods, with a particularly visible penalty for chunked HVOX because of v1's repeated spreading or interpolation. For dense HEALPix images, W-gridder plus mesh interpolation remains faster in these tests.

Sparse-domain runtime findings: When only 500 sky pixels are requested, HVOX-500MB performs both analysis and synthesis about one order of magnitude faster than W-gridder because it evaluates only the requested regions, while W-gridder still forms the full regular image. HVOX also significantly outperforms W-gridder plus interpolation on sparse HEALPix meshes. These are the paper's strongest runtime results and are relevant to sparse CLEAN models and calibration, but they do not establish the same advantage for dense imaging.

Real-data capability and timing: A qualitative demonstration loads an 8 h LOFAR-HBA Boötes-field measurement set with 24 core and 14 remote stations, synthesizes a 5 x 5 degree dirty image on an approximately 1.5-megapixel HEALPix mesh with HVOX-500MB, and writes FITS output in 38 s on the benchmark workstation. The paper shows the resulting image but reports no source-flux error, residual RMS, PSNR, SSIM, dynamic range, or matched W-gridder timing for this observation.

compute_cost: Grid-point throughput (Table 1): for the 4096 x 4096 grid and 129-pixel support benchmark, the NVIDIA Tesla C2070 CUDA implementation reaches 3413.5 Mpoints/s. Whole-node CPU results are 1408.9 Mpoints/s for a dual-socket Intel Xeon X5570, 393.7 Mpoints/s for a dual-socket Intel Xeon E5462, 372.2 Mpoints/s for a dual-socket AMD Opteron 2218, and 210.9 Mpoints/s for a Blue Gene/P PowerPC 450 node. Figure 4 also shows why per-core scaling is not a valid node estimate: the Intel E5462 falls from 163.25 Mpoints/s on one core to 393.73 Mpoints/s on all eight cores, rather than the approximately 1300 Mpoints/s implied by linear scaling, because the cores share a constrained memory bus.

Throughput versus support size (Figure 5): support sizes from 33 to 257 pixels are tested on the Tesla C2070 and dual-socket Xeon X5570. Throughput rises with support size: small supports are primarily limited by memory latency, while large supports are primarily limited by memory bandwidth. The benchmark was optimized for supports of 65 to 129 pixels, so the authors caution against reading the result as an inherent advantage of large support.

Arithmetic intensity and hardware utilization (Section 7): the complex single-precision inner loop is modeled as 8 floating-point operations and 24 bytes of memory traffic per grid point, approximately 0.3 single-precision flop/byte. The dual-socket Xeon X5570 achieves 11.3 single-precision Gflop/s, 6% of its 187 Gflop/s peak, and just over 50% of the approximately 2600 Mpoints/s bound implied by its nominal 64 GB/s memory bandwidth. The Tesla C2070 achieves 27.3 single-precision Gflop/s, about 2.7% of its 1.03 Tflop/s peak, and about 71% of the approximately 4800 Mpoints/s bound implied by 115.2 GB/s effective bandwidth with ECC enabled.

GPU overhead diagnostics (Section 7.2): at 129-pixel support, fetching 1032 bytes per convolution row through 128-byte cache lines requires nine loads, causing 120 bytes or about 12% overfetch. Gridding 160,000 samples requires 17,417 kernel launches to prevent overlapping convolution regions from being updated concurrently; launch barriers are identified as the secondary bottleneck after memory bandwidth.

ASKAP capacity estimates (Table 3): using the measured dual-socket Xeon X5570 throughput, the 30-arcsec spectral-line pipeline requires 1,156,290 Mpoints/s, about 820 nodes, and 76 double-precision Tflop/s peak; the 10-arcsec spectral-line pipeline requires 4,795,976 Mpoints/s, about 3404 nodes, and 319 double-precision Tflop/s peak; and the continuum pipeline requires 1,498,742 Mpoints/s, about 1063 nodes, and 100 double-precision Tflop/s peak. These are model-based capacity figures for the stated ASKAP configurations, not measured end-to-end pipeline runtimes.

Optimization gains (Section 8): favorable implicit on-the-fly sorting of samples by uvw coordinates improves CPU throughput by about 50% beyond Table 1, while an explicit sort yields 10-20%; software prefetch hints improve throughput by up to 15%, most strongly at small support.

W-stacking operation-count estimate (Section 8.3): relative to ASKAP W-projection supports that can exceed 100 pixels and require tens of thousands of grid-point updates per visibility sample, the memo estimates that W-stacking can use about 15-pixel support and reduce gridding operations by one to two orders of magnitude. It does not report a W-stacking implementation, wall-clock result, memory measurement, image comparison, or end-to-end accuracy benchmark.

Image fidelity: no reconstruction SNR, PSNR, RMSE, dynamic range, residual-image statistic, or deconvolution comparison is reported. The quantitative study concerns computational throughput, power, kernel support and truncation, hardware efficiency, and modeled capacity; image quality is not benchmarked.

rms: Evaluation scope and photometric caveats: The paper evaluates source morphology, integrated diffuse flux density, in-band spectral-index maps, residual-map rms, recovered contour levels, and computation. Flux is integrated within manually drawn source regions that approximately follow the 2-sigma contour in WSClean, using identical regions between algorithms for a given source and sub-band. WSClean restored images are normalized from Jy/beam to Jy/pixel by the restoring-beam area. No primary-beam correction is applied. The ASKAPsoft IAU Stokes-I convention is not corrected by the usual factor of two, so reported image fluxes are half those in ASKAPsoft mosaics. No flux-density uncertainties are reported because the Early Science and Pilot data had not been validated against standard flux catalogues.

Abell 3395 phoenix diffuse-flux comparison: Across the eight sub-bands centered at 887-1139 MHz, uSARA measures 29.3, 24.3, 14.5, 10.4, 13.5, 15.2, 7.3, and 7.4 mJy. WSClean restored images measure 30.2, 25.1, 25.2, 20.0, 25.7, 21.6, 10.0, and 8.3 mJy, while its smoothed models measure 27.2, 22.2, 23.8, 18.6, 23.4, 19.7, 9.5, and 7.1 mJy (Table 3). In the 887 MHz image, the uSARA source boundary follows about 1 microJy/pixel even though its calculated image-noise standard deviation is 6 microJy/pixel; the WSClean boundary is clearer at 2-3 times its measured 2 microJy/pixel residual rms. The lower restored-image flux agreement at higher frequencies is interpreted as residual-noise contamination and possibly a bias from monochromatic rather than wide-band cleaning, not established by a truth-based error metric.

PKS 2014-55 X-shaped galaxy flux and sensitivity: From 817 to 1069 MHz, uSARA integrated flux falls from 758.8 to 268.2 mJy, WSClean restored-image flux from 756.4 to 352.1 mJy, and WSClean smoothed-model flux from 743.7 to 308.4 mJy (Table 4). Except in the first sub-band, WSClean's restored-image flux is higher; smoothing its model brings the values closer to uSARA, consistent with the paper's residual-noise explanation. At 817 MHz, the uSARA source border is about 1 microJy/pixel against a calculated 6 microJy/pixel image-noise standard deviation, whereas WSClean's border is clearer at 3 times its measured residual rms of 1.6 microJy/pixel. Because the products have different effective resolution and no truth image, these contour levels are evidence of recovered low-surface-brightness structure rather than a controlled detection-limit measurement.

PKS 2130-538 Dancing Ghosts full-band and sub-band flux: On the comparatively clean SB9442 field, the 943 MHz full-band integrated flux is 117.2 mJy for uSARA and 115.5 mJy for both the WSClean restored image and smoothed model. Across 817-1069 MHz, uSARA falls from 131.0 to 101.8 mJy, WSClean restored images from 128.8 to 101.0 mJy, and WSClean smoothed models from 128.6 to 101.0 mJy (Table 6). This close agreement contrasts with the steeper, fainter sources in the calibration-artefact-dominated fields. Both full-band products recover the source boundary at 3 microJy/pixel. This is 3 times WSClean's measured 1 microJy/pixel residual rms but below uSARA's calculated 8 microJy/pixel image-domain noise standard deviation.

Metric limitations: The real-data study reports no PSNR, SSIM, normalized RMSE, source completeness, calibrated dynamic-range number, or visibility-residual statistic against known truth. Calibration artefacts extend up to degrees from bright sources in two fields, no direction-dependent recalibration is performed, and the regularization parameter is manually reduced from its noise-based heuristic for sub-band image quality. Claims of better fidelity and previously unseen structure are therefore supported by morphology, flux consistency, spectral trends, and residual-noise context, but not by a controlled truth-based benchmark.

snr: Reconstruction SNR (dB): SNR(x, x_gt) = −20·log₁₀(‖x_gt − x‖₂/‖x_gt‖₂), the primary image-fidelity metric vs. ground truth. QuantifAI's MAP reconstruction beats the wavelet-based MAP by 1.9–12.7 dB (average ~7 dB gain) across the dataset, and MAP consistently beats MMSE for both models.

Realistic ungridded-visibility experiment (MeerKAT, Table 6, M31 image): as synthesis time increases (1/2/4/8 h; 3×10⁴–2.4×10⁵ visibilities), MAP reconstruction SNR rises 25.29 → 28.39 → 31.94 → 34.42 dB, with reconstruction wall-clock time 17.0–105.3 s and UQ (fast pixel) wall-clock time only 0.28–1.26 s — full UQ-enabled reconstruction achievable in well under two minutes even at ~2.4×10⁵ visibilities. (2023) — an early version of the R2D2 paradigm — and AIRI (Terris et al. 2022), noting these DNN-based approaches "achieved similar or better performance than competing prior-based approaches whilst providing a significant acceleration," but does not benchmark QuantifAI numerically against R2D2/AIRI directly (no shared-dataset SNR comparison table).

credible_interval: Highest Posterior Density (HPD) credible regions: defined at credible level 100(1−α)% (Eq. 29–32); approximated analytically from the MAP potential via a concentration bound (Pereyra 2017), avoiding MCMC. Used as the basis for all downstream UQ tools.

Hypothesis testing of image structure: a region-of-interest is inpainted (Table 2) or Gaussian-blurred (σ=3.5 px, Table 3) to build a "surrogate" image, and its potential (f+g) is compared to the 99% HPD isocontour γ̂₀.₀₁ (α=0.01).
